content: 1. Smoking cigarettes significantly increases the risk of severe side effects when using the etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring, including heart attacks, blood clots, and strokes. This risk is particularly elevated in women over 35 years old who smoke heavily (15 or more cigarettes per day). If you use this vaginal ring, you should not smoke. 2. The etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring is prescribed to prevent pregnancy. It belongs to a class of medications known as combination hormonal contraceptives, which are used for birth control. Etonogestrel is a progestin, and ethinyl estradiol is an estrogen. 3. This vaginal ring prevents pregnancy by inhibiting ovulation (the release of an egg from the ovaries). It also alters the uterine lining to prevent implantation and changes the cervical mucus to block sperm from entering the uterus. 4. While the contraceptive ring is highly effective at preventing pregnancy, it does not protect against the transmission of HIV or other sexually transmitted infections. 5. The etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring is a flexible device that is inserted into the vagina and left in place for three weeks. After three weeks, it is removed for a one-week break, during which a menstrual period typically occurs. A new ring is then inserted after the one-week break. 6. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully. If you have any questions, consult your doctor or pharmacist. Use the ring exactly as directed. Do not use more than one ring at a time, and always insert and remove the ring according to the schedule provided by your doctor. 7. Insert and remove the ring on the same day of the week and at approximately the same time of day. Your menstrual period will likely begin 2–3 days after removing the ring and may continue throughout the one-week break. Insert a new ring at the end of the week, even if you are still bleeding. 8. Your doctor will advise you on when to insert your first contraceptive ring, depending on whether you were using another form of birth control, were not using birth control, or recently gave birth, had an abortion, or experienced a miscarriage. In some cases, you may need to use an additional method of birth control for the first seven days of using the ring. 9. Do not use a diaphragm as a backup method of birth control while the ring is in place. If the ring slips out, rinse it with cool or lukewarm water (not hot) and reinsert it as soon as possible. If the ring is lost, replace it with a new one and follow your original schedule for removal. 10. If the ring is out of your vagina for more than three hours, you must use a backup method of birth control until the ring has been in place for seven consecutive days. 11. To insert the ring, wash and dry your hands. Remove the ring from its foil pouch, but keep the pouch for disposal later. Choose a comfortable position (lying down, squatting, or standing with one leg raised). Squeeze the ring between your thumb and index finger and gently push it into your vagina. If you feel discomfort, push it further back. Wash your hands again after insertion. 12. To remove the ring, hook your index finger under the front rim or hold the rim between your index and middle fingers and pull it out. Place the used ring in the foil pouch and dispose of it in a trash can out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush it down the toilet. 13. Wait one week after removing the ring, then insert a new one following the same steps. 14. Inform your doctor if you are allergic to etonogestrel, ethinyl estradiol, or any other medications. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, and supplements you are taking, as some may interact with the ring. 15. Notify your doctor if you have a history of breast cancer, liver disease, blood clots, stroke, heart attack, high blood pressure, diabetes, or any other significant medical conditions. Also, inform your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. 16. If you forget to remove the ring on time but remember within one week, remove it immediately, wait one week, and then insert a new ring. If more than one week has passed, you may not be protected from pregnancy. Check for pregnancy and use a backup method of birth control until the new ring has been in place for seven consecutive days. 17. Minor side effects of the ring may include vaginal irritation, discharge, spotting, headache, nausea, weight changes, breast tenderness, or changes in sexual desire. Report any severe or persistent symptoms to your doctor. 18. Serious side effects, though rare, include leg pain, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headaches, vision changes, yellowing of the skin or eyes, and signs of depression. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience any of these symptoms. 19. The ring may increase the risk of liver tumors, breast or liver cancer, heart attack, stroke, or blood clots. Discuss these risks with your doctor. 20. Store the ring in its original packaging at room temperature, away from heat and moisture. Keep it out of reach of children. Dispose of expired or unused rings properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance. 21. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center or emergency services immediately. Symptoms of overdose may include nausea, vomiting, vaginal bleeding, or irregular periods. 22. Keep all medical appointments and undergo regular physical exams, including blood pressure checks, breast exams, pelvic exams, and Pap tests. Inform your doctor and laboratory personnel that you are using the vaginal ring before undergoing any tests.
